title: Latuda and Alcohol: Risks, the Food Rule, and Safe Timing
excerpt: Can you drink on Latuda (lurasidone)? How alcohol adds to its drowsiness, why skipping dinner breaks its 350-calorie food rule, timing, and warning signs.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Latuda? How alcohol and lurasidone interact, why the 350-calorie food rule matters on a night out, timing, and warning signs to watch for.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Latuda (lurasidone) and alcohol don't mix well, and the Latuda Medication Guide tells patients to avoid alcohol while taking it. Both slow your brain down, so together they can make you drowsier, dizzier, and clumsier than you expect. Latuda also has an unusual rule most medicines don't: it has to be taken with a real meal of at least 350 calories, or your body absorbs much less of it. A night of drinking instead of eating dinner can quietly break that rule. On top of both problems, alcohol tends to worsen the very bipolar depression and mood symptoms Latuda is usually prescribed for. This guide explains how the interaction works, what the food requirement means on a night out, how timing works, and the warning signs that need help right away.

**The quick rules:** Follow your label and avoid alcohol unless your prescriber has told you specifically what is okay for you. Always take your dose with a real meal of at least 350 calories; drinks don't count as that meal. Don't skip or stop Latuda so you can drink. Avoid grapefruit cocktails (Palomas, greyhounds, grapefruit juice mixers), because grapefruit can raise lurasidone levels. If someone who mixed Latuda and alcohol is very hard to wake, breathing slowly, fainting, or confused, call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and drug-label guidance. It is not a substitute for the doctor or pharmacist who prescribed your lurasidone and knows your diagnosis, dose, and other medicines. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist if** you take Latuda and drink at all, you want to know whether any amount of alcohol is okay for you, you take other sedating medicines (sleep aids, anxiety medicines, opioid painkillers, antihistamines, gabapentin), or you've noticed your drinking creeping up since starting it. **Get emergency help (call 911) if** someone who mixed Latuda and alcohol is hard to wake, breathing slowly, fainting, has a seizure, or has a very high temperature with stiff muscles and confusion. **If you're having thoughts of harming yourself, call or text 988** (the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline in the US) any time, day or night. Outside the US, contact your local emergency number or crisis line.

## What Latuda Is and Why People Take It

Latuda is the brand name for **lurasidone**, an atypical (second-generation) antipsychotic. Generic lurasidone has been available in the US since 2023, so you may see either name on your bottle. In the US it's approved for:

- **Bipolar depression** (the depressive episodes of bipolar I disorder), either on its own or alongside lithium or valproate, in adults and in children and teens aged 10 to 17
- **Schizophrenia** in adults and in teens aged 13 to 17

The word "antipsychotic" can be misleading. Many people taking Latuda have never had psychosis; they take it because it's one of a small number of medicines with good evidence for bipolar depression, which ordinary antidepressants often don't treat well. Lurasidone is also generally considered gentler on weight and blood sugar than some other drugs in its class, which is one reason prescribers choose it.

It works mainly by blocking dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors, with effects on several other serotonin receptors as well. That helps steady mood and thinking, but it also explains the side effects that matter when alcohol enters the picture: sleepiness, restlessness, nausea, and in some people dizziness when standing up.

## How Latuda and Alcohol Interact

There are three separate ways alcohol and lurasidone get in each other's way. It helps to keep them apart, because the advice for each is a little different.

### 1. The brain effects stack up

Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant. It dulls reaction time, judgment, balance, and alertness. Lurasidone's most common side effect in clinical trials was **somnolence**, the medical word for sleepiness and drowsiness. When you combine two things that each make you sluggish, the effects add together, and sometimes they add up to more than you'd predict from either alone.

In practice, people describe:

- Feeling much drunker than usual after a "normal" number of drinks
- Heavy drowsiness, or falling asleep somewhere unplanned
- Poor coordination and unsteady walking
- Foggy thinking and slower reactions, which matters a lot for driving
- Lightheadedness or nearly fainting when standing up quickly

That last one deserves its own mention. Like other antipsychotics, lurasidone can cause **orthostatic hypotension**, a drop in blood pressure when you stand up. Alcohol widens blood vessels and dehydrates you, which pushes in the same direction. Getting up from a bar stool or out of bed at 3 a.m. is when falls happen.

### 2. The food rule can quietly break

This is the part that is specific to Latuda, and it's the one most people miss.

Lurasidone is absorbed far better with food. In the manufacturer's studies, taking it with a meal roughly **doubled** the total amount absorbed and raised peak blood levels about **threefold** compared with taking it on an empty stomach. That's why the prescribing information tells you to take it **with food, at least 350 calories**. The studies also found that once you've eaten at least that much, the exact fat content of the meal didn't matter much.

Now picture a typical night out. You have drinks after work, snack lightly or not at all, and take your evening Latuda when you get home. You may have taken it on what is effectively an empty stomach. Alcohol calories aren't a meal, and there's no good evidence that a few beers or cocktails stand in for the food the label asks for. The result can be a lower dose than your prescriber intended. One night won't usually change much, but if it becomes a pattern, you're effectively taking a smaller, less predictable dose, and the medicine may seem to "stop working."

If you vomit after drinking, the problem gets worse, because some or all of your dose may come back up. Don't take a second dose to make up for it without asking your pharmacist; they can tell you what to do based on how long ago you took it.

For more on why skipping food changes how alcohol hits you in the first place, see our guide to [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach).

### 3. Alcohol pushes mood the wrong way

Most people taking Latuda are taking it for bipolar depression. Alcohol is a depressant in the mood sense too. It can give a short lift while you're drinking, then pull mood down over the following day or two as it wears off. Regular drinking is linked with more frequent and more severe mood episodes in people with bipolar disorder, worse sleep, and poorer response to treatment. Alcohol also lowers inhibitions, which is a real concern for anyone who has had suicidal thoughts.

Sleep is part of this. Alcohol might help you fall asleep faster, but it fragments the second half of the night and cuts into REM sleep. Disrupted sleep is one of the best-known triggers for mood episodes in bipolar disorder. Our guide to [alcohol and depression](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-depression) goes into the mood side in more detail.

## Lurasidone and Alcohol: Is There a Chemical Interaction?

People often ask whether alcohol changes lurasidone levels in the blood. Lurasidone is broken down mainly by a liver enzyme called **CYP3A4**. The label is strict about this enzyme: strong CYP3A4 blockers (such as ketoconazole or clarithromycin) can raise lurasidone levels many times over and should not be combined with it, and strong CYP3A4 boosters (such as rifampin or St. John's wort) can drop levels so low the drug stops working.

Alcohol itself is not a major CYP3A4 blocker or booster, so the main alcohol risk is the added effect on your brain, not a big swing in drug levels. The bigger chemical concern on a night out is actually your mixer:

- **Grapefruit and grapefruit juice** block CYP3A4 in the gut and can raise lurasidone levels. The label advises avoiding them. That includes Palomas, greyhounds, salty dogs, and any "grapefruit" seltzer made with real juice.
- **St. John's wort**, sometimes taken by people with low mood, can sharply lower lurasidone levels. It's sometimes sold in "mood support" or "relaxation" blends, so read labels.

If you take any other prescription, over-the-counter medicine, or supplement, ask your pharmacist to check it against lurasidone. It takes a few minutes and they're good at it.

## Can You Drink on Latuda at All?

The official answer from the Medication Guide is to avoid alcohol. In real life, some prescribers will discuss whether an occasional single drink might be acceptable for a particular patient who is stable, once they know how the medicine affects them. That's a conversation for you and your prescriber, not a rule you can apply from an article.

If your prescriber has said a small amount is okay for you, these habits lower the risk:

- **Eat a full meal first** and take your Latuda with that meal, as the label requires
- **Keep to the amount your prescriber agreed to**, if any, and sip it slowly, with water alongside
- **Skip grapefruit mixers** entirely
- **Don't drive** or do anything risky afterward, even if you feel fine
- **Stand up slowly**, especially at night
- **Notice how you feel the next day.** If your mood dips or restlessness flares, that's useful information to bring to your next appointment

What you shouldn't do is skip your dose so you can drink. That's covered in its own section below.

## How Long After Taking Latuda Can I Drink?

There's no safe waiting window. Lurasidone is taken once a day, and its half-life (the time it takes for the level in your blood to fall by half) is roughly 18 hours at common doses. Once you've been on it for a few days, the drug is in your system around the clock. Moving your drink a few hours away from your dose doesn't remove the interaction; you'd still be drinking with lurasidone on board.

The same logic applies the other way. If you drank last night and your dose is due this morning or this evening, the alcohol may be gone but the drowsiness, dehydration, and low mood from the drinking can linger. Take it with food as usual unless you're still intoxicated, unwell, or vomiting, in which case call your pharmacist first.

## What If You've Already Been Drinking and Your Dose Is Due?

This is a common, practical worry, and the best plan is one you've agreed with your prescriber before it happens. In general:

- **Don't double up** later, and don't take extra to "catch up"
- **If you're heavily intoxicated, very drowsy, or vomiting**, call your pharmacist or prescriber before taking it
- **If you're taking it, eat a real meal first.** Drinks don't count toward the 350 calories
- **Don't take other sedating things on top**, such as sleep aids, antihistamines like diphenhydramine, or leftover anxiety pills

Pharmacists answer questions like this every day without judgment. Many 24-hour pharmacies will talk you through it by phone.

## Latuda for Bipolar Disorder and Alcohol

Alcohol problems are common in people with bipolar disorder, far more common than in the general population, and many people with bipolar disorder say they've used alcohol to quiet anxiety, slow racing thoughts, or get to sleep. That's understandable. The trouble is that alcohol tends to make the illness harder to control over time, and it can mask whether a medicine like Latuda is actually helping.

If you're taking Latuda for bipolar depression, the most useful thing you can do is be honest with your prescriber about how much you drink. It isn't a moral question; it's a dosing and treatment question. They need to know whether a "not working" medicine is really not working, or whether alcohol, missed meals, or poor sleep are getting in the way.

Many people also take Latuda alongside lithium or valproate. Each of those has its own alcohol concerns. See our guide to [lithium and alcohol](/never-hungover/lithium-and-alcohol) if that's part of your regimen.

## Latuda for Schizophrenia and Alcohol

For people taking lurasidone for schizophrenia, the same sedation and food issues apply. Alcohol can also worsen psychotic symptoms, disturb sleep, and make it harder to keep a steady daily routine, including taking doses on time with meals. Teens taking Latuda shouldn't drink at all, both for legal reasons and because their brains and bodies respond more strongly to alcohol.

## Will Latuda Make a Hangover Worse?

There's no research looking at hangovers on lurasidone specifically, but you can reason it through. A hangover already involves fatigue, poor sleep, dehydration, nausea, headache, and low mood. Lurasidone's common side effects include sleepiness, nausea, and **akathisia**, an uncomfortable inner restlessness and urge to keep moving. Many people find that the morning after drinking on Latuda feels heavier and groggier than a hangover without it, and some notice restlessness or nausea flaring.

The bigger issue isn't the hangover itself; it's the mood dip that can follow a night of drinking, sometimes called "hangxiety." For someone with bipolar depression, a day or two of low mood isn't just unpleasant. It can be the start of a slide. If you notice that pattern, tell your prescriber.

## Latuda vs Other Antipsychotics With Alcohol

People sometimes ask whether Latuda is "safer" with alcohol than other antipsychotics. All of them carry warnings about alcohol, and the core advice is the same: avoid it or follow your prescriber's specific guidance.

There are some differences worth knowing:

- **Quetiapine (Seroquel)** is usually more sedating than lurasidone, so the drowsiness from mixing it with alcohol is often more pronounced. See our [Seroquel and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/seroquel-and-alcohol).
- **Aripiprazole (Abilify)** is usually less sedating but has its own concerns, including impulse-control effects. See our [Abilify and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/abilify-and-alcohol).
- **Lurasidone (Latuda)** sits in between on sedation, but it's the only one of these with a strict food requirement, which makes skipped dinners a particular problem.

Don't switch medicines on your own because one seems more "drink-friendly." These drugs are chosen for your diagnosis, side-effect profile, and history.

## Don't Stop Latuda to Drink

Some people skip a dose, or stop for a weekend, so they can drink without worrying. That's risky for a few reasons:

- Symptoms can return, sometimes quickly, especially in bipolar disorder
- Restarting can bring back early side effects like nausea, drowsiness, and restlessness
- Your prescriber loses a clear picture of whether the medicine works
- Missing doses on and off is one of the most common reasons treatment fails

If you want to drink at a wedding, a holiday, or a celebration, raise it with your prescriber ahead of time. They'd much rather have that conversation than have you stop your medicine without telling them.

## When to Get Help Right Away

Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if someone who has mixed Latuda and alcohol:

- Is very hard to wake, or can't be woken
- Is breathing slowly, irregularly, or making choking or gurgling sounds
- Faints, or collapses and doesn't come round quickly
- Has a seizure
- Is severely confused or agitated
- Has a high fever with very stiff muscles, sweating, and confusion (this can be a rare but serious reaction to antipsychotics called neuroleptic malignant syndrome)

While you wait, keep them on their side so they won't choke if they vomit, and don't leave them alone. Don't try to "sleep it off" for them or give them coffee or a cold shower.

Contact your prescriber soon (same day or next day) if you notice:

- New or worse depression, or mood swinging toward feeling unusually high, wired, or reckless
- Thoughts of self-harm (call or text **988** right away in the US)
- Restlessness you can't sit still through, or new stiffness, shaking, or unusual muscle movements
- Repeated dizziness or near-fainting when you stand
- Finding that you're drinking more than you planned, or more than before you started treatment

## The Bottom Line on Latuda and Alcohol

Latuda's label says to avoid alcohol, and there are good reasons behind it. Alcohol adds to lurasidone's drowsiness and dizziness, it works against the mood benefits you're taking the medicine for, and a night of drinking instead of eating can quietly undercut the 350-calorie food rule that Latuda depends on to absorb properly. Grapefruit mixers add a separate chemical risk. If you want to drink at all, talk to your prescriber first, always take your dose with a real meal, and never skip doses to make room for alcohol.

## A Note on Supplements, Including DHM

Because this is a hangover site, we're often asked whether supplements can make drinking safer on a medication like Latuda. They can't. **There is no good evidence that DHM (dihydromyricetin), or any other hangover supplement, reduces the sedation, dizziness, or mood effects of combining alcohol with lurasidone**, and DHM hasn't been studied alongside antipsychotics. Lurasidone is also sensitive to anything that affects its liver enzyme, and the interaction profile of most supplements hasn't been tested against it.

If you take Latuda, no supplement makes alcohol safer with it, so check with your prescriber or pharmacist before adding anything, including hangover products. Our [alcohol and medications guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-medications) summarizes how the main drug classes interact with alcohol, and our guides to [Seroquel and alcohol](/never-hungover/seroquel-and-alcohol) and [Abilify and alcohol](/never-hungover/abilify-and-alcohol) cover two other antipsychotics in the same family.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Latuda?**

The Latuda Medication Guide tells patients to avoid drinking alcohol while taking it. Both lurasidone and alcohol act on the brain, so together they can add up to more drowsiness, dizziness, poor coordination, and slower thinking than either one alone. Alcohol also tends to worsen the depression and mood swings Latuda is often prescribed to treat. If you want to know whether any amount is okay for you, ask the prescriber who knows your diagnosis, dose, and other medicines.

**What happens if you drink on lurasidone?**

Most commonly, people feel more sedated, unsteady, or lightheaded than they expected from the amount they drank, especially when standing up. Some people notice more restlessness (akathisia) or nausea the next day. Over days and weeks, regular drinking can undo the mood benefits of the medicine, disturb sleep, and make it harder to take doses consistently with food. Very heavy drinking on top of lurasidone raises the risk of falls, accidents, and dangerous over-sedation.

**How long after taking Latuda can I drink?**

There is no safe waiting window. Lurasidone is taken once a day and its half-life is roughly 18 hours at common doses, so the drug is in your body around the clock once you are on it. Spacing a drink a few hours away from your dose does not remove the interaction. The label's advice is simply to avoid alcohol while you take it.

**Why does Latuda have to be taken with food?**

Lurasidone is absorbed much better with a meal. In the manufacturer's studies, taking it with food roughly doubled the amount absorbed and raised peak levels about threefold compared with taking it fasting. The label says to take it with at least 350 calories of food. If you skip dinner and have drinks instead, you may take your dose on what is effectively an empty stomach and absorb noticeably less of it.

**Do alcohol calories count toward Latuda's 350-calorie food requirement?**

There is no good evidence that they do. The absorption studies used real meals, and the label wording is about food. Beer, wine, or cocktails are not a substitute for eating. If your dose is due with dinner, eat an actual meal of at least 350 calories with it, whether or not you have been drinking.

**What if I drank and my Latuda dose is due?**

Don't double up later and don't take extra to make up for anything. If you only had a small amount and feel normal, your prescriber or pharmacist can tell you in advance how they want you to handle this situation. If you are heavily intoxicated, very drowsy, or vomiting, call your pharmacist or prescriber before taking it. If someone is hard to wake, breathing slowly, fainting, or confused after mixing the two, call 911.

**Can I stop taking Latuda so I can drink at a party?**

No. Skipping doses or stopping on and off can let bipolar depression or psychotic symptoms come back, and restarting can bring back early side effects. Talk to your prescriber about your drinking plans instead. They can tell you what is realistic and safe for you.

**Does grapefruit or alcohol change Latuda levels?**

Grapefruit and grapefruit juice can raise lurasidone levels because they block CYP3A4, the liver enzyme that breaks it down, and the label advises avoiding them. That includes grapefruit cocktails such as a Paloma or a greyhound. Alcohol itself is not a major CYP3A4 blocker, so the main alcohol problem is the added effect on your brain, not a big change in drug levels.

**Does DHM make it safe to drink on Latuda?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM reduces the sedation, dizziness, or mood effects of combining alcohol with lurasidone, and it has not been studied with antipsychotics. DHM is a supplement studied mainly for alcohol metabolism and hangovers, mostly in animals. If you take Latuda, ask your prescriber or pharmacist before adding any supplement, DHM included.
